title: Forest bathing

fn.en: Talk about the natural world and about probability.

sub.en: How sure is the speaker? That is what changes.

items.q: This trend ___ spread around the world — every study points the same way.
items.why: definitely goes after will and marks near-certainty.

items.q: The percentage ___ rise to about ninety-two per cent by 2030.
items.why: be likely to + infinitive. The verb be is required.
may / might / could all mean “possibly” — less certain than will.

items.q: It ___ even stop you getting ill, though nobody is sure yet.

items.why: probably goes before won’t and after will.

items.q: People who live near green spaces ___ be physically active.
It ___ well become popular in Europe too.
items.why: might well = there is a fairly strong chance. It is stronger than plain might.
doubt is a state verb, so the simple form is used.

It probably won’t rise. / I doubt it.

tts: Good afternoon, and welcome to Science Matters. Recent research suggests that people are spending less time outdoors.
One study looked at visits to national parks in the United States, Japan and Spain, and found that the number of visits had gone down by eighteen per cent since the late 1980s.
So why do we stay indoors so much?

Well, it may be that rather than enjoying nature, we prefer to sit in front of a screen. People in the US now spend around eight and a half hours a day looking at one, and this trend will definitely spread as smartphones become more common.

Another explanation is that more people live in cities. In 1950, seventy-nine per cent of the UK population lived in cities, and that percentage is likely to rise to around ninety-two per cent by 2030.

Yes. People who live near green spaces are more likely to be physically active. And researchers in Edinburgh say that people’s brains actually change in natural environments, reducing stress and improving mood.

items.q: What has happened to national park visits since the late 1980s?
o: They have fallen by about eighteen per cent

items.q: How sure is the reporter that screen time will spread worldwide?
o: Almost certain — she says it will definitely spread

items.q: What does she say about the UK city population by 2030?
o: It is likely to reach about ninety-two per cent

tts: Shinrin-yoku, or forest bathing, is simply visiting a forest and walking slowly, taking in everything you see, hear and smell.
Scientific research shows that walking in the forest for thirty minutes will reduce depression and lower your blood pressure.
They even think it might prevent you from becoming ill.
It seems that the trees give off chemicals which help to keep you healthy. One study showed a fifty per cent increase in the white blood cells needed to fight illness after a two-hour walk.
The Japanese government has already built forty-eight official forest-bathing trails, and they say they will definitely build another fifty-two within the next ten years.
South Korea has already started building its own centres, and other countries, like Finland, may soon follow.

items.s: Forest bathing means walking slowly and paying attention to everything around you.
A thirty-minute forest walk is said to lower blood pressure.
Scientists are certain that forest bathing prevents illness.
Japan has already built more than forty official trails.
The reporter says other countries definitely will not follow.

write.q: Write four predictions about your city, your country or your own life in the next ten years. Make each one a different level of certainty: one almost certain, one likely, one possible, one unlikely.
plan: likely — is likely to / there’s a good chance
unlikely — probably won’t / I doubt it
write.model: In the next ten years the number of cars in my city will definitely go up — three new blocks are being built on my street alone, and every flat comes with a parking space. There’s a good chance the bus network will be extended at the same time, because the council has already published a plan. The old park behind the station might well be rebuilt; there has been talk about it for years, and this time somebody has bought the land. What probably won’t change is the traffic on Bukhar Zhyrau. People have been promising to fix that since before I was born, and I doubt it will happen now.

speak.q: Say four predictions out loud, from the most certain to the least. Change the words each time — do not use will four times.
speak.model: The number of cars will definitely go up. There’s a good chance the bus network will be extended, because the plan is already published. The park behind the station might well be rebuilt. But the traffic on Bukhar Zhyrau probably won’t change — honestly, I doubt it ever will.
